## GENESIS 27:1-23 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — *“When Isaac was old and his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see, he called his older son Esau…”*

- Isaac was likely about 137 years old at this point (Luther's calculation). He would live to 180, so he had 43 more years — his sense of approaching death was premature. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- Ellicott calculates Isaac at 117, noting the term “old” is used loosely; he reckons 63 more years of life. The eye failure may have resulted from an acute disorder that made Isaac despondent about his health. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- Gill likewise sets Isaac at 137, the age at which Ishmael died (Gen 25:16), which may have prompted Isaac to think his own end was near. The dimness of his eyes is noted not merely as a sign of old age but as providentially ordered so that Jacob might receive the blessing. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that Isaac’s failing eyesight and the recollection of Ishmael’s death at 137 occasioned his suspicion that his end was near, though he lived either 43 or 63 years longer depending on the chronology adopted. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 2 — *“Look, I am now old, and I do not know the day of my death.”*

- Isaac’s words reflect genuine uncertainty about his lifespan. Gill comments that everyone knows they must die but no one knows the day or hour; an old man especially must live in constant expectation of death. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes Isaac had become “manifestly apprehensive of the near approach of dissolution.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 3 — *“Take your weapons—your quiver and bow—and go out into the field to hunt some game for me.”*

- The Hebrew word for “quiver” (*teli*) is a *hapax legomenon* (appearing only here), derived from a root meaning “to hang” — thus “that which is suspended.” The Targum and Syriac render it “sword.” Ellicott concludes it was some sort of hunting implement, possibly a hanger (a short sword). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- Gill also notes the ambiguity: Onkelos and Jarchi interpret it as a sword, while others maintain “quiver.” Both would be necessary for hunting. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary explains “take me some venison” is literally “hunt for me hunting” — i.e., the produce of hunting. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 4 — *“Then prepare a tasty dish that I love and bring it to me to eat, so that I may bless you before I die.”*

- David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal) argues Isaac was not merely interested in food but in Esau’s identity as a “manly hunter.” He could not taste the difference between wild game and domestic goat, suggesting it was the thought of Esau as a mighty hunter that attracted him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- Guzik further says Isaac insisted on blessing Esau despite God’s revealed choice of Jacob (Gen 25:23), Esau’s despising of his birthright (25:29-34), and his pagan marriages (26:34-35). Isaac “rejected godly thinking and spiritual wisdom.” The secrecy of the planned blessing indicates Isaac knew it was wrong. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- Ellicott notes that on rare occasions an Arab sheik would taste flesh flavoured with almonds, pistachio nuts, and raisins, making it hard to distinguish kid from antelope. He sees the meal as preparatory to a prophetic act: “under the influence of the Spirit, and in expectation of death,” the patriarch decided which son would inherit the birthright. Isaac was “resisting the Spirit,” for the clear prophecy had said “the elder should serve the younger.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- Gill: Isaac’s request was a test of Esau’s filial affection before bestowing the blessing. The blessing concerned not merely temporal goods but the descent of the Messiah and possession of Canaan. Gill suggests Rebekah had not told Isaac the oracle about the elder serving the younger, or he had forgotten or misunderstood it. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary: “notwithstanding the oracle (Gen 25:23) uttered so many years ago, Isaac appears to have clung to the belief that Esau was the destined heir of the covenant blessing; *quaedam fuit coecitatis species, quae illi magis obstitit quam externa oculorum caligo* (Calvin) — ‘it was a kind of blindness that hindered him more than the outward dimness of his eyes.’” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 5 — *“Now Rebekah was listening to what Isaac told his son Esau…”*

- Guzik says the text does not necessarily imply spying; Rebekah may have casually overheard the conversation. Her readiness with a plan, however, suggests scheming. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- Ellicott proposes Rebekah was possibly present when Isaac gave the order, and Isaac may even have wished her to know his determination. The words “filled her with dismay.” Had her faith been “pure and exalted,” she would have trusted God to fulfil His word without her help. “But here the fault began with Isaac, and Rebekah probably considered that she was preventing a grievous wrong.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- Gill notes simply that Providence ordered Esau’s departure to the field to allow time for Jacob to obtain the blessing. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)

### vv. 6-7 — *“Behold, I overheard your father saying to your brother Esau, ‘Bring me some game … so that I may bless you in the presence of the LORD before I die.’”*

- Rebekah adds the phrase “before the LORD” (Jehovah) which is not recorded in Isaac’s original speech in v. 4. Ellicott says it is unreasonable to accuse her of inserting words — more of Isaac’s address was spoken than is recorded. These words had a meaning to Jacob (the covenant with Jehovah) that they did not bear for Esau, who cared mainly for temporal benefits. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary likewise defends Rebekah against the charge of invention: the phrase may have been implied though not expressed by Isaac. It points to the idea that Rebekah regarded Isaac as “the instrument of the living and personal God, who directed the concerns of the chosen race.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 8 — *“Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you.”*

- Guzik: “Instead of trusting God to fulfill His promise (Gen 25:23), Rebekah used manipulation and scheming.” He quotes Spurgeon: “Good men have gone very wrong when they have thought of aiding in the fulfillment of promises and prophecies. See how Rebecca erred… We had better leave the Lord’s decrees in the Lord’s hands.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- The Pulpit Commentary observes that Jacob was not a lad but a grown man of about 77, making him “rather an accomplice than a tool.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### vv. 9-10 — *“Go out to the flock and bring me two choice young goats, so that I can make them into a tasty dish for your father…”*

- Ellicott says two kids would be about equal to one antelope. After Isaac ate, a feast for the household likely followed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- Gill: the Jewish writers note that in her marriage contract, Isaac had allowed Rebekah to take two kids of the goats every day, giving her the right to do this without her husband’s permission. Jarchi says the taste of a kid is like the taste of a young roe. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- Rebekah knew Isaac couldn’t tell the difference between her cooking and wild game. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)

### v. 11 — *“Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned.”*

- Jacob’s only concern was whether the plan would succeed, not whether it was right. Guzik calls this pragmatism — “when we are willing to abandon the question of right and wrong, and when our only concern is what works.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- The Pulpit Commentary: Jacob was “not yet such an adept at trickery as he afterwards became, and … if he had no scruples of conscience … was yet averse to being detected in his frauds, as deceivers usually are.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 12 — *“What if my father touches me? Then I would be revealed to him as a deceiver, and I would bring upon myself a curse rather than a blessing.”*

- The Hebrew word for “deceiver” (*meta‘ta‘*) conveys the idea of a scorner or one who mocks. The Pulpit Commentary suggests both senses — mocking his aged father’s infirmities and deceiving him — should be included. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)
- Jacob’s fear of a curse rather than a blessing shows he understood the seriousness of what he was about to do. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Baptist Garner-Howes commentary notes Jacob was “apprehensive” — his concern was being caught, not the morality of the act. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-27.html)

### v. 13 — *“Your curse be on me, my son. Just obey my voice and go get them for me.”*

- Guzik/Spurgeon angle: Rebekah’s bold statement may be viewed as faith in the divine promise — she was confident no curse would come. Yet the means she used were carnal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- The Pulpit Commentary takes a nuanced view: “Tempted to regard Rebekah’s words as the utterance of a bold and unscrupulous woman … we ought perhaps to view them as inspired by faith in the Divine promise.” Calvin and others held this view. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)
- Ellicott notes the irony: “No curse followed upon their conduct; but, on the contrary, Isaac acknowledged the substantial justice of the act … and confirmed Jacob in the possession of the blessing (Gen 27:33). It seems strange, nevertheless, that neither of them had any scruples at the immorality of the deed.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- Gill notes the Targum of Onkelos renders it: “to me it has been said in prophecy, that the curses shall not come upon thee, my son.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 14 — *“So Jacob went and got two goats and brought them to his mother, who made the tasty food his father loved.”*

- Once Jacob overcame his fear of being caught, he was a willing participant. Guzik: “Rebekah manipulated both Isaac and Jacob, but Jacob was a willing partner.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)

### v. 15 — *“And Rebekah took the finest clothes in the house that belonged to her older son Esau, and she put them on her younger son Jacob.”*

- The “goodly raiment” (Hebrew *bigdei*) may have been special garments. Ellicott suggests Esau may have held a sort of priestly office in the household; the clothing was “something special, and such as was peculiar to Esau: for ordinary raiment, however handsome, would not have been kept in the mother’s tent.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary dismisses the rabbinic idea that these were sacerdotal robes of the firstborn priesthood as “devoid of proof.” They were more likely “festive garments of the princely hunter.” The verb is in the *hiphil*, implying Jacob actively clothed himself — he was not purely involuntary. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)
- Gill reports the Jewish tradition that these were the garments of Adam, which Esau obtained by killing Nimrod. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 16 — *“She also put the skins of the young goats on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.”*

- In hot countries, goat coats are far less thick and coarse. Some Oriental goats (camel-goats) have soft, silky black wool sometimes used as a substitute for human hair (cf. Song of Solomon 4:1). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary: these were “not European, but Oriental camel-goats, whose wool is black, silky, of a much finer texture.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)
- The Baptist Garner-Howes commentary: these were “camel-goats, with long, fine, black wool which was soft like human hair.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-27.html)

### v. 17 — *“Then she handed her son Jacob the tasty food and bread she had made.”*

- The Pulpit Commentary notes Jacob “forthwith proceeded on his unholy errand.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 18 — *“So Jacob went to his father and said, ‘My father.’ ‘Here I am!’ he answered. ‘Which one are you, my son?’”*

- Isaac’s immediate question “Who are you, my son?” shows suspicion from the start. Guzik says Isaac was old and blind but not without discernment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- The Pulpit Commentary: “He thought he recognized the voice of Jacob; his suspicions were aroused; he knew the crafty disposition of his younger son too well; and he felt the duty of extreme carefulness.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)

### v. 19 — *“Jacob said to his father, ‘I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may bless me.’”*

- Guzik calls this “a clear lie, with Jacob deliberately deceiving his father, and doing it for selfish gain.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- Gill similarly rejects attempts to excuse Jacob: some (like Jarchi) say Jacob only said “I” not “I am Esau,” but Gill calls this insufficient — “it is an answer to Isaac’s question, with a design to deceive him.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary lists Jacob’s three distinct lies in this verse: claiming to be Esau, claiming to have done as Isaac commanded, and claiming to bring venison. “One lie commonly requires another to support or conceal it.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)
- The Baptist Garner-Howes commentary: “This was an unjustified lie. But it was in keeping with the character of Jacob, which was evident in his name: ‘supplanter,’ or ‘heel-catcher.’” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-27.html)
- Ellicott notes Jacob’s command “arise, sit and eat” shows Isaac was not bedridden but simply reclining; the Hebrews sat at meals at this period. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)

### v. 20 — *“‘How did you ever find it so quickly, my son?’ ‘Because the LORD your God brought it to me,’ he replied.”*

- Guzik: “Jacob, the scoundrel, did not hesitate to give credit to God as part of his deception.” Jacob justified any lie because he (rightly) knew God wanted him to have the birthright. “He probably told himself that it was all for a righteous cause.” Guzik adds: “Jacob was not the last among God’s people to use the promise and calling of God as an excuse for sin.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- Ellicott: “Jacob does not keep up his acting well here, for it was not in accordance with Esau’s character to see anything providential in his success in hunting. This may have helped to arouse Isaac’s suspicions.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary uses strong language: Jacob replied “with daring boldness,” “with consummate effrontery,” “not without perjury,” and even “with reckless blasphemy.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)
- Gill observes Jacob said “the LORD thy God” (not “my God” or “our God”), which some think was to cover the deceit based on Esau being an idolater; Gill suggests rather that “Jacob had not the confidence to call the Lord his God with a lie in his mouth.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Baptist Garner-Howes: “Jacob compounded his deception by saying that Jehovah Elohim had prospered his search.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-27.html)

### v. 21 — *“Then Isaac said to Jacob, ‘Please come closer so I can touch you, my son. Are you really my son Esau, or not?’”*

- Isaac’s suspicions persisted — the quick success plus the pious language were unlike Esau. He resorts to the sense of touch as a more reliable test. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- Ellicott: Isaac was surprised both by the pious answer and the short delay. Though the twins’ voices had some similarity, Isaac detected the difference. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)

### v. 22 — *“So Jacob came close to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, ‘The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.’”*

- Isaac’s famous line captures the tension: his ears told him one thing, his hands another. Guzik notes he trusted touch over hearing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
- Gill: Isaac “might imagine there might be an alteration in Esau’s voice, coming in haste and weary from the fields; yet, as there could not be any deception in his feeling, he thought it safest to trust to that.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- Matthew Henry (referenced via StudyLight) draws a spiritual analogy: “His voice is Jacob’s voice, but his hands are Esau’s. He speaks the language of a saint, but does the works of a sinner; but the judgment will be, as here, by the hands.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-24.html)
- The Baptist Garner-Howes: “Jacob was unable to disguise his voice, but the feel of his hands partially allayed the suspicions of Isaac.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-27.html)

### v. 23 — *“Isaac did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau; so he blessed him.”*

- Dr. Constable’s Expository Notes (Evangelical) clarifies that “so he blessed him” is proleptic — it refers forward to the blessing pronounced in vv. 27-29, not a separate blessing at this moment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-27.html)
- Gill: Isaac “intended and determined within himself to bless him, for the blessing was not given till afterwards; unless this is to be understood of a common blessing, congratulating him on the quick dispatch.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Isaac must either have forgotten the heavenly oracle (Gen 25:23) or not attached the same importance to it as Rebekah, or thought it concerned descendants rather than the sons personally. “It is hard to credit that Isaac … believing it, deliberately allowed paternal partiality to … endeavor to reverse, the will of Heaven.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/27.htm)
- Guzik emphasizes that each person in this drama “acted in man-centered wisdom and energy, not according to divine or spiritual wisdom.” All four — Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Esau — “did not trust each other. Even worse, they did not trust the Lord.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)

## TRADITIONAL READINGS — Where Protestant Traditions Diverge

Given tool limits, only partial tradition coverage was possible. Here is what the sources yielded:

### Baptist
- **Gill (Particular Baptist, Calvinistic):** Firmly condemns Jacob’s lies as sin — rejects Jarchi’s attempt to excuse Jacob’s “I am” as mere evasion. Emphasises Providence: Isaac’s blindness was “so ordered in Providence” that the blessing might fall to Jacob. Notes that the blessing concerned not just land but “the descent of the Messiah from him and his seed.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/27.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Calls Jacob’s lie “unjustified” but notes it was in keeping with his name (“supplanter”). Emphasises that Rebekah “sought to do God’s will by her own devices” and was “unwilling to wait for God to overrule Isaac’s wrong design.” This “hindered the full, free working of God’s power to overcome the errors of men.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-27.html)

### Reformed / Spurgeon
- Quoted within the Enduring Word commentary: Spurgeon says “the whole story reflects no credit upon any of the persons concerned” and warns against aiding the fulfilment of prophecy by wrong means. As soon as Isaac realised he was wrong, “he does not think for a moment of retracting what he has done — he feels that the hand of God was in it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)

### Anglican
- **Ellicott:** Emphasises Divine election (citing Romans 9:10-13). Contrasts Abraham, who obeyed God’s choice (though with a heavy heart, Gen 21:11), with Isaac, who “even struggled against God’s will.” The blessing was a prophetic act under the Spirit’s influence, and Isaac “resisted the Spirit.” Ellicott defends Jacob on one point: “he sought no earthly good … All that was Isaac’s he resigned to Esau.” The wrong was in using “miserable artifices to do that which should have been left to God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-27.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Treats the passage as a cautionary tale about pragmatism and man-centered wisdom. Each character acted without trusting God. Key emphasis: “the worst aspect of this all is they seemed to regard the covenant blessing as magical, as something detached from God’s wisdom and will.” The blessing only mattered if God in heaven honoured it. Guzik stresses divine sovereignty: God’s will was done despite human opposition. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/)
